newsitem.title: BARBADOS: Clinton attacks U.S. House juvenile crime bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton attacks U.S. House juvenile crime bill.

text.p: President Clinton Saturday attacked juvenile crime legislation passed by the Republican-controlled House of Representatives, saying it ignores his own prescription for stopping youth violence.

"I challenge Congress to pass a real juvenile justice bill, one that's tough on gangs and tough on guns and is serious about the kind of prevention efforts we know will work," he said in his weekly radio address.

The House approved juvenile justice legislation Thursday by a 286 to 132 vote, with 77 Democrats joining 209 Republicans. It would allow juveniles as young as 13 to be tried as adults for violent crimes and drug offences.
The bill would only apply to federal crimes, which account for a small percentage of overall offences. But supporters said it was needed to encourage states to also try violent juveniles as adults.

Clinton, on a week-long tour of Mexico, Costa Rica and Barbados, complained the House bill ignored the anti-crime measures he proposed in legislation sent to Congress in February to crack down on youth gangs.

Clinton, who made fighting juvenile crime and gangs a top priority of his second term, did not specifically threaten a veto of the House bill. A similar bill is pending in the Republican-led Senate. Clinton and the Republicans have fought frequently over the direction of crime-fighting measures.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton would "fight hard for our strategy. We think over time we'll be able to win the case on the merits of our argument."

The president's legslation would "declare war" on gangs with new prosecutors and tougher penalties. It would extend the Brady Bill handgun control law to bar someone who commits a crime as a juvenile from buying a gun as an adult.

It would also require that child-safety locks be sold with guns to try to prevent accidental shootings and it would help keep schools open after hours, on weekends and in the summer to give children a place to go to instead of the streets.
Clinton said the House bill does not ensure the anti-gang prosecutors, is weak on guns, and does not fund his initiatives to keep schools open.

Perhaps most troubling, he said, the House bill rejects his call to cut off young people's access to guns, which he said was now the third leading cause of death for young people between the ages of 13 and 24.
"To me, a juvenile justice bill that doesn't limit children's access to guns is a bill that walks away from the problem," Clinton said.
As for the child-safety locks, Clinton cited a National Institute of Justice survey that said 185 children died in 194 because of accidental shootings.
"Now, if we can have safety precautions to prevent children from opening bottles of aspirin, surely we can have the same safety precautions to prevent children from using guns," Clinton said.
Clinton taped his radio address Friday aboard Air Force One while sitting on the tarmac at the airport in San Jose, Costa Rica.
